rail_guard.text: Holyhead. The end of the line, and the start of Ireland. Mind the gap, mind the gull.
Hop aboard. The Wildlore rail runs to any town you have visited on this island. Where to?

then.text: Ticket? Lovely. Laminated, even. Somebody loves you. The Ulysses sails for Dublin whenever the tide and the timetable agree. Fancy a crossing?

else.text: Sorry, love. No ticket, no crossing. The harbour board checks, and the harbour board has a clipboard.
I hear a certain professor in Macclesfield posts them to people who've seen off a gentleman in a Panama hat, down in Cornwall. Perhaps that's you, in time.

then.text: Gale's up, so the ferry might be a bit late. Or bouncy. Probably both. Ginger biscuit?
Fog on the Irish Sea. The ship's got radar, so it's fine. The seagulls have nothing.
Night sailing, is it? Three hours to Dublin and you'll be there by morning. Bring a pillow.

ticket_clerk.text: Three hours to Dublin. We have a lounge, a cafe, a shop, and a deck for people who've decided they'd like to be a figurehead.
Holyhead is the main ferry port for the Irish Sea. On a good day it's a good deal calmer than the passengers.

then.text: Gale's blowing. FitzRoy would've hoisted the storm cone for this one. I'm off home for a cuppa.
Rain doesn't bother the fish. They're wet already. I'm the only one complaining.

old_fisherman.text: The breakwater's the best place to fish. You can see the whole bay. And the whole bay can see you.
In 1859 the Royal Charter was wrecked off Anglesey in a hurricane. That's how the weather forecast got going, more or less. Admiral FitzRoy started his storm warnings two years later.

then.text: Glaw! That means rain. You'll learn that word fast up here, cariad.
Bore da! Early sun over Holyhead Mountain. Lovely, it is, before the ferry crowd turns up.

welsh_local.text: Bore da! That's good morning. We say 'Caergybi' for Holyhead. 'Caer' is fort, and 'Cybi' is the saint. Fort of Cybi.
Mind, the signs say both, Welsh and English. If you can pronounce Caergybi, you can have a biscuit.

museum_curator.text: The museum has models of the ferries that sailed from here. They look the same to me, but I'm told the funnels differ.
Holyhead has had a harbour for two thousand years. The Romans, the Vikings, the Irish and the railway all came this way. We got good at waving.

then.text: Fog round the Roman walls. Very atmospheric. I'm writing it all down. Too much detail, probably.

fort_student.text: The fort walls at Caer Gybi are 4th-century Roman, nearly four metres thick in places. They still stand around the church.
I wrote an essay about it. The marker said 'too much detail'. There's no such thing. There's only insufficient walls.
